title: Piezo: GHz ultrasonic through-silicon acoustic vias replace HBM data TSVs
idea: Pattern thin-film ScAlN bulk-acoustic transducers on each thinned DRAM die; data rides as 5-10 GHz longitudinal ultrasound pulses straight through the bonded silicon stack, each die's transducer tuned to its own frequency band so one acoustic column serves 16 dies. No holes are drilled, so TSV keep-out zones and TSV-induced yield loss disappear.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): recovers TSV+KOZ area (~5-10% of die) and part of the 20-30% stack yield loss; per-column bandwidth ~10-20 Gb/s, so best for command/address, ECC and sideband lanes first.

title: Silicon transparency: infrared optical vias broadcast commands through HBM stacks
idea: Silicon is transparent above 1.1 um, so a 1.3 um VCSEL on the base die shines vertically through 16 thinned DRAM dies, each carrying a small partially absorbing Ge photoconductor window that taps ~5% of the light; command/address and clock are broadcast optically to all dies at once instead of through TSV columns.
why: Removes C/A and clock TSVs and their capacitive load (facts 5, 6); one emitter replaces 16 drivers; ~30-40% fewer TSVs, sub-pJ/bit broadcast.

title: Magnetostriction: magnetoelectric nano-antennas give chiplet memory links without interposer wires
idea: FeGaB/AlN magnetoelectric antennas radiate at their GHz acoustic resonance rather than their electromagnetic wavelength, making them ~100x smaller than patch antennas; arrays on memory and compute chiplets talk wirelessly through mold compound with no interposer routing.
why: Removes silicon interposer (CoWoS capacity and cost) for low-to-mid bandwidth memory chiplets; packaging capex down; ~1-3 pJ/bit target.

title: Mott transition: NbO2 steep-threshold receivers enable 80 mV memory I/O swings
idea: Put NbO2 threshold-switch elements at the front end of DRAM I/O receivers; their abrupt insulator-metal transition acts as near-infinite-gain slicing so a 60-100 mV interposer swing switches cleanly, replacing 300-400 mV swings and biased sense amplifiers.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5) and voltage floor (fact 10): I/O CV^2 falls ~16x at 4x lower swing; HBM PHY from ~3.5 to <1 pJ/bit if sub-ns switching and endurance hold.

title: Coulomb blockade: thousand-electron charge-packet signaling read by single-electron sensors
idea: Encode each interposer bit as a ~1,000-electron charge packet clocked down a short low-capacitance line and sense it with room-temperature single-electron transistors built from sub-2 nm silicon islands whose conductance swings per elementary charge.
why: Moves ~0.16 fC per bit instead of ~40 fC (100 fF x 0.4 V): ~250x less charge, attacking pJ/bit (fact 5) at the extreme; thermal noise and reliability make it speculative.

title: Direct tunneling: oxide tunnel-bond hybrid bonding without metal-to-metal contact
idea: Cap both Cu bond pads with 1-1.5 nm of bond dielectric so current crosses by direct tunneling (ohmic-like at mV) plus capacitive coupling for AC; pads no longer need to expand and fuse, so dishing tolerance loosens and anneal drops below 200 C, protecting DRAM retention.
why: HBM stacking yield and pitch (fact 6): relaxes CMP/dishing specs that drive hybrid-bond yield loss, enables sub-um pitch at low thermal budget; pad tunnel resistance must stay low.

title: Spin Hall oscillators: frequency-multiplexed carriers put eight channels per interposer wire
idea: Pt/NiFe spin-Hall nano-oscillators, each <1 um^2 and current-tunable from 5-25 GHz, act as tiny carriers; eight differently tuned oscillators share one interposer line and spin-diode detectors demultiplex them at the memory die.
why: Interposer wire density and beachfront (facts 5, 6): 8x fewer wires per unit bandwidth, smaller interposer; nW output power and phase noise are the risks.

title: Electrochromism: zero-holding-power optical shutters reconfigure rack memory-pool topology
idea: WO3/NiO electrochromic shutters placed in front of a fixed fan-out optical mesh open or close specific memory-to-host light paths; they switch in ~100 ms and hold state with no power, letting a rack reassign terabytes of pooled DRAM between servers as workloads shift.
why: Raises usable memory supply by cutting stranded DRAM (often 20-30% idle per server) with no new bits; slow switching fits allocation timescales.

title: Ion migration: electroformed silver filaments grow and repair vias after stacking
idea: Bond dies through a thin chalcogenide solid-electrolyte layer between coarsely aligned pads; a post-bond forming pulse drives Ag+ ions to grow filaments bridging whichever pads face each other, and any open or degraded bond found in field test is re-grown by another pulse.
why: HBM yield loss of 20-30% (fact 6): turns opens into repairable defects and relaxes alignment to a few um; filament current capacity and long-term stability are the risks.

title: Thermal hysteresis: NiTi shape-memory microcontacts make HBM stacks reworkable
idea: Replace permanent microbumps with NiTi micro-springs that clamp pads at operating temperature and release when the stack is heated through the austenite transition, so one failed DRAM die in a 12-high stack is lifted out and replaced instead of scrapping the stack and its GPU.
why: HBM compound yield and scrap (fact 6): converts a $1,000+ package loss into a single-die swap; contact resistance and ~20 um pitch limit it.

title: LC resonance: adiabatic energy-recovery memory buses recycle interposer line charge
idea: Make interposer line groups part of resonant LC tanks with on-package thin-film inductors so charge sloshes between line and inductor instead of dumping to ground; data is encoded in the phase/polarity of the resonant swing, resonant clocking applied to data.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5) and CV^2 floor (fact 10): recovers 60-80% of line energy, HBM bus ~3.5 to ~1 pJ/bit; constrains encoding to near-periodic signaling.

title: Pockels effect: thin-film lithium niobate modulators bonded on HBM base die
idea: Heterogeneously bond thin-film LiNbO3 microring modulators onto the HBM base die so the stack speaks optics directly at ~0.5-1 V drive and ~50 fJ/bit modulator energy; memory sits meters from the GPU over fiber with no electrical SerDes.
why: Frees memory from GPU beachfront and interposer area; ~1 pJ/bit end-to-end vs 3-4 pJ/bit electrical HBM at 10x+ the reach; enables pooled HBM.

title: Kerr soliton microcomb: one shared laser powers all memory chiplet optics
idea: A single SiN Kerr microcomb per rack generates 64-128 phase-locked wavelengths distributed over fiber as an optical power utility; memory chiplets carry only modulators and detectors, no lasers, removing per-chiplet laser cost, heat and failure.
why: Makes optical memory links (fact 5) cheap at DRAM volume; removes lasers from hot memory packages; 64 wavelengths x 32 Gb/s per fiber.

title: Superconductivity: liquid-nitrogen memory pool with YBCO lossless backplane traces
idea: House pooled DRAM at 77 K where YBCO-coated tape traces carry signals with near-zero resistance and dispersion, while cold DRAM retention rises by orders of magnitude so refresh nearly disappears and the leakage tail collapses.
why: Refresh tax (fact 3, 16-33% idle power) and data-movement loss (fact 5); the ~10 W/W cryocooler overhead must be beaten by refresh and I/O savings at pool scale.

title: Resonant tunneling: InP RTD terahertz transceivers link GPUs and memory towers
idea: Resonant-tunneling-diode oscillators at 300-600 GHz with on-chip slot antennas give 50-100 Gb/s line-of-sight links between a processor and surrounding memory towers in a sealed package or across adjacent boards, avoiding fine-pitch wiring.
why: Interposer, TSV and beachfront limits (facts 5, 6): memory scales out in 3D around a GPU; ~1-2 pJ/bit target.

title: Phonon bandgap: superlattice thermal barrier lets DRAM sit atop hot logic
idea: Insert a 50-100 nm WSe2/MoS2 van der Waals stack or W/Al2O3 nanolaminate with cross-plane thermal conductivity <0.1 W/mK between logic and DRAM, while copper thermal pillars route logic heat sideways; DRAM stays below 85 C despite face-to-face 3D bonding.
why: Enables DRAM-on-logic with the shortest wires (<0.2 pJ/bit, fact 5) without the 2x refresh penalty above 85 C (fact 3).

title: Peltier effect: thin-film thermoelectric base die cools taller HBM stacks
idea: Embed thin-film Bi2Te3/Sb2Te3 Peltier couples in the HBM base die under hot spots, actively pumping heat out of the DRAM core layers into the cold plate, so 16-24-high stacks stay within thermal limits at the normal 64 ms refresh rate.
why: HBM height ceiling (density per footprint, fact 6) and refresh (fact 3): spends a few W of TEC power for 30-50% more bits per stack.

title: Electrowetting liquid metal: Galinstan microchannel vias are stress-free and reconfigurable
idea: Fill vertical microchannels with gallium-alloy liquid metal instead of solid Cu, removing CTE stress and keep-out zones; electrowetting electrodes along spare channels move metal plugs to connect or disconnect lanes, giving in-field lane repair.
why: TSV keep-out area and stress-induced yield loss (fact 6); repair without heavy spare-TSV overprovisioning; Ga attack on Al/Cu needs barriers.

title: Magnetic induction: cored micro-coils shrink inductive die-to-die links to 5 um
idea: Add electroplated CoZrTa thin-film magnetic cores to stacked micro-coils so the coupling coefficient rises from ~0.1 to >0.5, allowing ThruChip-style inductive vertical links at 5 um pitch through 32 thinned dies with no TSVs.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield (fact 6): contactless stacking with no via etch/fill; core loss at multi-GHz is the risk.

title: Stochastic resonance: noise-assisted bistable receivers detect 30 mV memory signals
idea: Drive an array of bistable comparators with deliberately injected uncorrelated noise so a sub-threshold 30 mV signal biases their switching statistics; majority-summing 16 comparators recovers each bit at low BER on a fraction of today's swing.
why: I/O CV^2 energy (facts 5, 10): ~100x lower swing energy minus comparator overhead, net ~3-5x pJ/bit on short interposer links.

title: Acousto-optics: Bragg-cell beam steering time-shares one optical link across memories
idea: A surface-acoustic-wave acousto-optic deflector on a lithium niobate interposer steers a host's free-space beam among 32 memory chiplets in ~100 ns by changing the RF drive frequency, forming a solid-state switched memory fabric with no electrical crossbar.
why: Data movement and pooling (fact 5): one transceiver serves 32 memory targets, cutting SerDes count and stranded memory; switch time suits page migration, not per-access.

title: Pyroelectricity: self-powered per-bank thermal telemetry drives fine-grained refresh
idea: Deposit thin AlScN pyroelectric patches over each DRAM bank in the stack; temperature changes generate charge with no bias, integrated and read via spare sideband lanes, so the controller refreshes each bank at its true temperature instead of the stack worst case.
why: Refresh (fact 3): most banks run far cooler than the hottest spot; 20-40% fewer refreshes and recovered bandwidth.

title: Capillarity: water-droplet self-alignment speeds die-to-wafer hybrid bonding
idea: Pattern hydrophilic bond sites inside hydrophobic surrounds, dispense a nanoliter water droplet, and drop DRAM dies coarsely; surface tension pulls each die to <200 nm alignment before direct bonding, so placement tools run 10x faster at coarse accuracy.
why: HBM assembly capital and throughput (facts 4, 6): hybrid bonders are slow and costly; capillary alignment cuts bonder capex per stack.

title: Total internal reflection: roll-to-roll nanoimprinted polymer waveguide flex for memory optics
idea: UV-nanoimprint single-mode fluorinated-acrylate waveguides on a moving polyimide web, with tapered adiabatic couplers that mate evanescently to SiN chips; the flex carries 64+ optical lanes from memory modules to the processor package.
why: Optical memory interconnect (fact 5) at cents per lane instead of dollars per fiber-array assembly; board-scale memory pooling at ~1 pJ/bit.

title: Dielectrophoresis: fluidic self-assembly drops memory chiplets onto roll-to-roll interposers
idea: Flow shaped DRAM chiplets in a carrier fluid over a printed polyimide interposer web whose electrodes form dielectrophoretic traps matching the chiplet outline; chiplets lock into sites at tens of thousands per minute, then printed solder joins them.
why: Packaging capex and throughput (facts 4, 6): replaces serial pick-and-place, making many-small-die memory modules (higher die yield) cheap; site-fill yield is the risk.

title: Melting-point depression: low-temperature sintered copper nanoink printed redistribution layers
idea: Inkjet/EHD-print 3-5 um Cu nanoparticle lines whose size-depressed melting point lets them sinter below 200 C under photonic flash, forming fan-out RDL on molded memory panels without lithography, sputter or plating tools.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4): replaces litho+plating for fan-out lines; no silver; low thermal budget protects retention; 2-3x bulk resistivity is acceptable for fan-out.

title: Acoustoplasticity: room-temperature ultrasonic bonding of DRAM chiplets on moving webs
idea: Use the Blaha acoustic-softening effect: 40-60 kHz ultrasound softens copper bumps so DRAM chiplets bond to printed Cu-on-polyimide in ~100 ms at room temperature, synchronized with web motion like RFID strap bonding.
why: Assembly capex and thermal budget (fact 6): no reflow ovens or thermocompression bonders; heat-free bonding avoids retention damage; pitch limited to ~30-40 um.

title: Latent heat: printed phase-change heat buffers flatten HBM burst temperatures
idea: Screen-print a microencapsulated phase-change composite melting at ~75 C into a lid cavity over the HBM stack so AI burst heat is absorbed at constant temperature, keeping DRAM under the 85 C double-refresh threshold during peaks.
why: Refresh (fact 3): avoids 2x refresh rate in bursts with a cheap printed paste; buffers only seconds-scale transients.

title: Magnetic dipole chaining: field-aligned nickel-particle printed films for fine-pitch z-interconnect
idea: Print a curable polymer loaded with nickel microparticles on R2R film; an applied magnetic field chains the particles into vertical columns at ~5 um pitch before UV cure, giving an anisotropic z-conductor that attaches memory dies to printed interposers without bumps.
why: Packaging cost and pitch (fact 6): bumpless, solderless die attach on R2R lines at 5-10x finer pitch than conventional ACF.

title: Mott transition: printed VO2 off-die ESD clamps strip I/O pad capacitance
idea: Print VO2 nanoparticle-ink clamps on the package substrate at each memory I/O; an ESD surge drives them metallic so they shunt the current, letting on-die ESD diodes (100-300 fF per pad) shrink to minimum size.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): pad capacitance dominates short-reach I/O CV^2, so ~50% less pad C cuts I/O energy in proportion; also frees periphery area (fact 7).

title: Coulomb blockade: printed gold-nanoparticle films as threshold bus terminations
idea: Print ligand-capped 2-4 nm Au nanoparticle arrays whose collective Coulomb-blockade threshold keeps them insulating for small signals but conducting beyond a size-tuned voltage; as terminations they absorb reflections only during overshoot instead of burning static ODT current.
why: I/O power (fact 5): on-die termination burns a large share of DDR interface power; nonlinear termination could halve it; threshold uniformity is speculative.

title: Johnsen-Rahbek electroadhesion: programmable roller stamps transfer only known-good DRAM dies
idea: A roller stamp with an addressable electrode array energizes Johnsen-Rahbek electroadhesion only under dies that passed wafer test, lifting thousands of known-good DRAM chiplets per revolution and printing them onto a moving interposer web.
why: Assembly throughput and yield (fact 6): massively parallel known-good-die transfer with no pick-and-place capex.

title: Capillary wicking: roll-embossed two-phase cooling film laminated onto memory stacks
idea: Hot-emboss micro-pillar wicks and vapor channels into copper-clad polymer film on R2R lines, then seal and laminate it as an ultra-thin vapor chamber over HBM; capillary pumping returns condensate with no pump.
why: Thermal height limit and refresh (facts 3, 6): 10-20 C lower hot spots allow taller stacks; replaces machined vapor chambers at a fraction of cost.

title: Dielectric waveguiding: extruded polymer mm-wave tubes carry memory traffic one meter
idea: Continuously extrude low-loss PTFE/PE dielectric waveguide ribbons and launch 140-220 GHz carriers from CMOS transceivers into them, giving 100+ Gb/s per tube over 1 m with no lasers for board-to-board memory-pool links.
why: Data movement (fact 5): cheaper than optics and longer than copper at ~1-2 pJ/bit; enables disaggregated DRAM pools that raise utilization.

title: Phase-gradient metasurfaces: printed reflectarrays steer wireless memory links inside servers
idea: Roll-print copper patch metasurfaces with fixed phase gradients on films lining chassis walls, redirecting 60-140 GHz beams between memory boards and processors so wireless links get high-gain non-line-of-sight paths.
why: Memory expansion and pooling without cables or backplanes; costs cents per square meter; each chassis layout needs its own pattern.

title: Electroluminescence: printed perovskite LED arrays drive thousands of slow parallel lanes
idea: Print perovskite micro-LED and photodiode arrays with ~10 um pixels on interposer film and image one onto the other through a fiber bundle; 10,000 lanes at 200 Mb/s give 2 Tb/s with plain NRZ and no SerDes.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): wide-and-slow optical lanes avoid SerDes power (sub-pJ/bit); perovskite stability at 80 C and speed are the risks.

title: Photoconductivity: printed photoconductor pads receive a flood-lit optical reference clock
idea: Flood a whole memory board with a 100-500 MHz modulated light reference from one source through a printed light-guide film; printed photoconductor pads at each memory chip pick it up as a low-jitter reference for local PLLs, removing board clock trees and buffers.
why: I/O energy (fact 5): removes clock distribution power and skew margin; printed parts cost cents; photoconductor speed limits it to reference rates.

title: Displacement current: printed high-k nanocomposite pinless capacitive memory connectors
idea: Print a BaTiO3-polymer high-k layer over connector pads on module and motherboard flex so signals couple capacitively across a thin gap with no metal contact, decoded by pulse-mode receivers; modules slide in with no pins to wear or corrode.
why: Module cost and signal integrity (fact 5): removes stubs and pin capacitance, enabling cheap hot-swap memory expansion; DC power still needs contacts.

title: Moire magnification: printed interference marks enable nanometer roll-to-roll overlay
idea: Print paired gratings of slightly different pitch on each layer of an R2R interposer; their Moire fringes magnify misalignment 100-1000x and cameras feed real-time web registration actuators, enabling 1-2 um lines with ~100 nm overlay.
why: Brings R2R from ~20 um to near-silicon-interposer density for memory fan-out (facts 4, 6) at a fraction of the capex.

title: Microphase separation: block copolymer templates print 20 nm wiring on rolls
idea: Coat a block copolymer over a nanoimprinted guide pattern on R2R film; it self-assembles into 20-40 nm lamellae that template electroless metal lines, giving ultra-dense, low-cost local redistribution wiring between memory and processor.
why: Interposer wire density (fact 6) without litho tools (fact 4); large-area defectivity is the risk; local wiring only.

title: Shape-memory polymer: printed thermally releasable underfill makes chiplet modules reworkable
idea: Print an underfill made of shape-memory epoxy that is rigid and stress-relieving below 120 C but softens and contracts past a 160 C transition, so a failed memory chiplet can be lifted off a printed interposer and replaced.
why: Chiplet package yield and scrap (fact 6): reworkability saves the whole module; thermal-cycling reliability must be proven.

title: Self-focusing photopolymerization: light writes its own waveguide from fiber to chiplet
idea: Dispense photosensitive resin between a flex-waveguide or fiber end and a memory chiplet's grating coupler; light launched through the fiber self-focuses and polymerizes a bridging waveguide along its own path, giving automatic sub-um alignment.
why: Fiber attach is the cost and throughput bottleneck of optical memory links (fact 5); a printable resin step replaces $1M active-alignment stations.

title: Ballistic transport: printed aligned-nanotube repeaters make long flex memory links
idea: Shear-align printed semiconducting carbon-nanotube films on R2R flex to form short-channel transistor repeaters every few mm along memory interconnect, enabling GHz signaling over 10 cm of flex without silicon.
why: Data movement over printed substrates (fact 5): an active printed interposer at R2R cost; nanotube purity and alignment are high risk.

title: Elastic buckling: roll-printed kirigami interposers pop up into 3D memory cages
idea: Print wiring on a pre-cut kirigami polyimide film; releasing pre-strain buckles it into a 3D cage that surrounds a processor with memory chiplets on all sides instead of along one edge.
why: GPU memory beachfront and interposer area (facts 5, 6): 3-4x more memory adjacency per processor from flat R2R manufacturing; thermal and mechanical robustness risk.

title: Volume holography: printed photopolymer holograms fan one laser to 64 chiplets
idea: Record multiplexed volume holograms in R2R-coated photopolymer film so one input beam diffracts into 64 precisely aimed spots on memory chiplet detectors, distributing broadcast data, clock or optical power across a module with no waveguides.
why: Optical broadcast and laser sharing (fact 5): one source feeds many memory chiplets; holograms are contact-copied at cents; alignment tolerance is the risk.

title: Aerodynamic focusing: aerosol-jet printed staircase edge wiring replaces stack TSVs
idea: Stack DRAM dies offset like a staircase and aerosol-jet print conductive traces over printed dielectric ramps down the exposed edges, so every die connects to the base die without a single TSV.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): reclaims TSV area and yield loss and removes via etch/fill tools; lower edge bandwidth suits capacity-optimized (CXL) stacks.
